newsitem.title: INDIA: India liberalisation not enough to attract FDI - RBI.
newsitem.headline: India liberalisation not enough to attract FDI - RBI.

text.p: India's economic liberalisation policies would not by itself lead to increased foreign direct investment (FDI), the country's central bank said.

These would have to be supplemented with measures to increase the size of the domestic market, improve productivity and infrastructure, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) said in a research report made available to Reuters on Friday.
The study by the Development Research Group of the RBI's Department of Economic Analysis and Policy, analysed the patterns of FDI flows into India between 1991 and 1995.
It said that FDI has moved into priority areas such as power generation, oil refinery, telecommunications, electronics and food processing where domestic investment is inadequate.
It said actual FDI inflow into India has fallen short of expectations and that the country had not been as successful as other major FDI-seeking Asian countries such as China.
One reason could be that economic liberalisation policies by themselves may not be enough, the study suggested.

"The main factor determining FDI inflows into a developing country is seen to be the prevailing economic environment, understood to include, domestic market size, levels of infrastructure development, cost conditions and broad macro-economic conditions."

The study said the irrelevance of further liberalisation was underlined by the fact that the current Indian policy of openness in economic policy was equal to that of other countries more successful in attracting FDI.
"In fact, from the policy perspective, India scores over China, which has been attracting the major share of FDI flows into the developing world," it said.

This was despite Chinese requirements that all FDI proposals get approval on a case-by-case basis while India had a scheme for automatic approval of foreign equity upto 51 percent in listed priority industries, the study said.

The study noted that in general foreign investors tended to move into areas which have growing domestic markets such as consumer goods and services despite uncertainties in getting approvals for investments in such non-priority areas.
Such aspects underscored the relevance of strategic policy intervention by the government, the study said.
The case for enlarging the scope and speed of the ongoing liberalisation process to attract FDI was therefore not very strong, it said.
